input.description: We represent Barham Investments, LLC, owner of a four-story glass-showcase car dealership near Keystone Avenue and 96th Street in Indianapolis, as the condemnee in a City of Carmel eminent domain action in Marion Circuit Court for a roundabout interchange project. Carmel took a small triangular strip in fee, an access-control line, and a temporary construction right-of-way; court-appointed appraisers set compensation at $163,000, which Barham rejected on the ground that the taking, together with Carmel's separate condemnation and closure of Threel Road, extinguished the dealership's ingress-egress easement and main entrance. Carmel's motion for partial summary judgment on the access issue was denied and the case is set for a jury trial on just compensation.
input.documentText:
The City of Carmel used its power of eminent domain to convert the intersection of Keystone Avenue and 96th Street into a roundabout interchange ("the Project"). Barham Investments, LLC ("Barham"), owns a car dealership, whose main entrance was on Threel Road, near the intersection that Carmel needed to acquire to complete the Project. In April of 2018, the trial court entered an agreed order of appropriation and appointment of appraisers ("the Agreed Order"). Barham considered the appraisers' valuation of the Property to be too low because the taking allegedly extinguished its easement in Threel Road.

In December of 2017, Carmel exercised its eminent-domain power to construct the Project. In doing so, Carmel filed a condemnation complaint in which it claimed that it needed to acquire three separate property interests from Barham, including 0.017 acres in fee simple, an access-control line, and 0.0111 acres in a temporary right-of-way for construction ("the Property"). Barham objected to Carmel's complaint, claiming that Carmel had "failed to properly identify all of the ownership interests being extinguished by the taking. Namely, the easement rights of the landowner to access and use Threel Road." Barham's car dealership consisted of a four-story, glass-enclosed car showcase and a guest-entry area positioned towards the dealership's main entrance on Threel Road, which had run alongside Keystone Avenue. However, Carmel had already condemned Threel Road in a separate cause: Carmel v. County Line Owners Association, Inc., Case No. 49D02-1801-PL-003953 ("the County Line Action"). So, Carmel did not name Threel Road in its condemnation complaint or seek to acquire it.

In April of 2018, the trial court denied Barham's objection and the parties entered into the Agreed Order, which authorized Carmel's acquisition of the Property. Barham consented to the "Appropriation of Real Estate as sought in the Complaint." In the Agreed Order, the trial court ordered that the taking consisted of "frontage along Threel Road" and that the access-control line "will be the new west property line of the subject, and the intent is to limit any access to the west of this line towards Keystone." The Agreed Order did not include any acquisition of Threel Road.

Later that month, the trial court instructed the three court-appointed appraisers to appraise the Property described in Carmel's complaint. In June of 2018, the appraisers assessed the total just compensation due to Barham to be $163,000.00. Barham disputed the appraisers' valuation, alleging that the "total damages assessed to [Barham] are too low[,]" and requested a jury trial.

In January of 2021, Carmel moved for partial summary judgment, arguing that Barham was not entitled to compensation for its loss of access to Threel Road. In its motion, Carmel relied on the County Line Action, which, in part, had granted Carmel "the total acquisition of Threel Road" in April of 2018. In March of 2022, the trial court denied Carmel's motion for partial summary judgment, finding that "there are genuine issues of material facts that remain unresolved." In doing so, trial court explained that Carmel "cite[d] no law that definitively foreclose[d] [Barham]'s arguments for compensation for the elimination of the ingress and egress easements or the diminution of value that the loss ha[d] caused to the value of their properties."

Carmel argues that it "did not in this case acquire Threel Road or an easement in Threel Road"; consequently, this case should be controlled by the traffic-flow rule and the trial court erred in leaving the question of whether there had been the loss of an easement for the jury. For its part, Barham argues that the trial court properly denied Carmel's motion for summary judgment because this case involves an easement and a substantial change in how the Property is used.

Barham claims that Carmel owed it compensation for the taking of its ingress and egress easement in Threel Road. At some point, Barham acquired a common Non-Exclusive Easement over, across and under the Easement Property [(i.e., Threel Road)] for pedestrian and vehicular traffic, sewer lines, water lines, fire protection lines and other utilities. The purpose of such easement is to provide the owners, lessees and occupants of such property within County Line Commercial Park ingress and egress to such property, and to provide the means for the owners of property within County Line Commercial Park to service their property with water mains, sanitary sewer mains, and fire protection water lines. The Agreed Order appropriated a "fee simple area that is a triangular strip of land off of the northwest side of the lot, adjacent to Threel Road" and a "temporary right of way of 0.111 acres at the southwest corner of the site to remove the drive entrance and complete drainage work."

In the County Line Action, the trial court granted Carmel, among other things, "the total acquisition of Threel Road[,]" causing "Threel Road [to] be permanently closed as a result of the Project." Barham maintains sufficient access to run its business via Aronson Road.

outcome.description: After a May 2022 jury trial the Marion Circuit Court entered judgment on a $2.4 million verdict for Barham and denied Carmel's motions to correct error, for new trial, and for remittitur. The Court of Appeals reversed on October 30, 2023, holding Barham had no compensable easement interest in Threel Road (already extinguished in the County Line condemnation) and that the access change was non-compensable under the ingress-egress and traffic-flow rules, and remanded with instructions to grant Carmel partial summary judgment on that issue.
outcome.finalNote: Reversed and remanded; no final figure yet.

input.description: We represent Navient Solutions, LLC, the tenant (and plaintiff) under a 2012 commercial lease of the 85,563-square-foot Blue Wing office building at the Iron Hill Corporate Center in Newark, Delaware, in a breach-of-lease action in the Delaware Superior Court against the landlord, BPG Office Partners XIII Iron Hill LLC. Navient sued in April 2020 for $503,822.72, the unamortized cost of a cooling tower it replaced in 2019, which the landlord conceded before trial; the landlord counterclaimed for $817,845 in repair and replacement costs for heat pumps, rooftop air units, a transformer and elevators, and each side seeks prevailing-party fees under the lease. A three-day bench trial limited to the counterclaim was held in May 2022 with expert testimony on both sides, post-trial briefing and oral argument are complete, and the matter is awaiting the court's post-trial decision.
input.documentText:
Plaintiff/Counterclaim Defendant Navient Solutions, LLC (“Navient”) filed this commercial landlord-tenant breach of contract action. Navient is a Delaware limited liability company and was formerly known as Sallie Mae, Inc. Defendants/Counterclaim Plaintiffs BPG Office Partners XIII Iron Hill LLC and Office Partners XIII Iron Hill LLC (collectively, “BPG”) are two Delaware limited liability companies. BPG asserted a breach of contract counterclaim against Navient.

The Iron Hill Corporate Center is a three-building office complex in Newark, Delaware (the “Office Complex”). On November 20, 2012, Sallie Mae, Inc. (now Navient) and BPG entered into a commercial lease agreement for the Blue Wing with Navient as the tenant and BPG as the landlord (the “Lease Agreement”). The Blue Wing is the subject of this action; it is a three-floor building with approximately 85,563 rentable square feet.

Navient services student loans; in connection with that operation, Navient operated a call center at the Blue Wing. Navient fully vacated the Blue Wing by the end of 2019, which gave Navient enough time to remove furniture and equipment before the Lease Agreement terminated on February 29, 2020. BPG’s counterclaim in this action relates to four areas of Blue Wing equipment and maintenance: (1) a transformer, (2) heat pumps, (3) rooftop fresh air units, and (4) elevators.

The total unamortized cost of replacing the cooling tower and its component parts was $503,822.72. On January 28, 2020, Navient demanded $503,822.72 from BPG for the then-unamortized cost of the cooling tower replacement. BPG denied its obligation to reimburse the cooling tower costs until shortly before trial, when BPG acknowledged it owed Navient that amount.

On October 13, 2014, a transformer blew; that transformer was installed at the time the Blue Wing was constructed. Later in the day on October 14, 2014, the blown transformer was replaced. The concrete pad on which the replacement transformer rested was fitted with metal shims in an attempt to level the transformer in compliance with applicable code and the transformer manufacturer’s installation instructions. The replacement transformer had a larger capacity than the original but had a two-position switching arrangement as opposed to the original four-position switch. Navient paid $70,000 for the replacement transformer. Nevertheless, BPG claims it is entitled to $140,000 because Navient did not meet its contractual obligation to install a four-position switch and a permanent level concrete pad under the transformer.

After the Lease Agreement ended, BPG employed Edward Levering and Keith Nelson, both from Air Management and Design LLC, to survey approximately 123 heat pumps at the Blue Wing. Again, Mr. Levering recommended that any heat pump that exceeded the 19-year median useful life should be replaced. Mr. Levering’s calculation for the total cost of replacement was $405,800. Mr. Levering identified 25 of 123 heat pump units as non-operational at the time of his evaluation. Mr. Levering stated 11 of the 25 non-operational heat pump units were below their median life expectancy, and these 11 heat pumps should be repaired (rather than replaced) at an estimated cost of $28,750. Mr. Levering stated 14 of the 25 non-operational heat pumps exceeded their median life expectancy and should be replaced at a cost of $107,100. Navient called its own expert, Howard Alderson, an engineer who testified there was no reason to replace a heat pump based solely on its age. Mr. Alderson testified the heat pumps at the Blue Wing as of 2021 were well maintained.

The Blue Wing has two “Dectron rooftop makeup air units.” These rooftop air units provide makeup air for the Blue Wing, but BPG’s inspection showed the units were not operational when Navient left the Blue Wing because the controls never were programmed for the new controllers installed on the rooftop air units. Mr. Frenck, however, conceded these rooftop air units could be repaired rather than replaced. Mr. Frenck’s estimated cost to repair both rooftop air units totaled $8,400, while BPG’s estimated cost to replace the rooftop air units is between $217,200 and $240,000.

Navient contracted with ThyssenKrupp Elevator Corporation to maintain the elevators at the Blue Wing during the lease. Instead, BPG alleges that in September 2020 it had to repair a bracket in one elevator for $3,345.

Navient sued BPG in April 2020. Navient’s sole cause of action alleged BPG breached the Lease Agreement by failing to reimburse Navient for the unamortized cost of replacing the cooling tower. BPG’s counterclaim alleged Navient breached the Lease Agreement by failing to: (1) maintain, repair, and/or replace heat pump units; (2) maintain, repair, and/or replace the rooftop air units; (3) properly replace the blown transformer and install a permanent pad to level the transformer; and (4) maintain and repair the elevators. BPG requested $817,845 from Navient. Before trial, BPG agreed Navient is owed $503,822.72 for the replacement of the cooling tower. BPG continued, however, to maintain its counterclaim. The trial was limited in scope to BPG’s counterclaim.

BPG contends the Court should enter judgment in its favor in the amount of $817,845, itemized as: (1) $434,500 for heat pumps, (2) $240,000 for rooftop air units, (3) $140,000 for the transformer and pad, and (4) $3,345 for the elevators. It is now undisputed that Navient is entitled to $503,822.72 for the unamortized cost incurred when it replaced the cooling tower at the Blue Wing. What remains in dispute is whether that amount should be set-off, in whole or in part, by BPG’s counterclaim. Navient contends BPG did not prove either liability or damages with respect to its counterclaim. Navient alternatively argues BPG’s counterclaim relating to the transformer is barred by Delaware’s three-year statute of limitations because BPG knew about the replacement transformer in October 2014.

outcome.description: The Superior Court entered post-trial judgment for Navient in $503,822.72 (the conceded cooling-tower reimbursement) less $79,650 awarded to BPG on its counterclaim ($71,250 to repair 25 non-operational heat pumps and $8,400 to repair two rooftop air units), a net principal of $424,172.72 plus prejudgment interest from March 17, 2020; BPG's transformer and elevator claims failed. Navient was held the prevailing party entitled to its attorneys' fees and expenses under lease section 28(q) (amount not stated). This is the trial-level decision; no appeal is reflected in the source.
